title: Locke's Influence
orientation: This short chapter closes Russell's treatment of Locke by tracing the international afterlife of his philosophy. Russell divides post-Lockean European thought into two broad, rival streams -- one descending from Locke's empirical, piecemeal method through Berkeley, Hume, Bentham, and the philosophical Radicals; the other descending from Descartes through Spinoza, Leibniz, and Kant -- and argues that the crucial contrast between the two lies as much in method (inductive vs. deductive system-building) as in doctrine, with consequences reaching into modern politics and ethics.
historical_background: Locke's philosophy reached France chiefly through Voltaire, whose Lettres philosophiques interpreted English ideas to French readers already predisposed, by their opposition to an 'antiquated, corrupt, and effete despotism,' to admire England as the home of freedom; Hume's later residence in France reinforced this influence. In England, Locke's immediate philosophical heirs (Berkeley, a bishop uninterested in politics; Hume, a Tory) took little interest in his political doctrines until the French Revolution forced philosophers to take political sides, though Russell notes the purely philosophical, empirical tradition (visible even in the young Shelley) continued unbroken. Kant's Critique of Pure Reason (1781) revived the rival, Continental rationalist tradition, partly because German universities had never fully accepted empiricism and partly because, after 1792, empiricism was blamed for the excesses of the French Revolution.
philosophical_problems: What distinguishes the 'British' (empirical, piecemeal, inductive) philosophical method from the 'Continental' (rationalist, systematic, deductive) method, and what are the consequences of each?

Is there a genuine, principled connection between a philosopher's theory of knowledge and their political outlook, or is the correlation between empiricism/rationalism and liberalism/conservatism merely historical accident?
Does grounding ethics in pleasure/happiness (the empiricist, utilitarian line) or in something 'noble' beyond happiness (the rationalist, idealist line) better serve human welfare in practice?
Can Locke's individualist political philosophy, built for an age of citizens and small states, still address a world of vast organizations, corporations, and warring nation-states?

philosophers_discussed.name: John Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Treated throughout as the fountainhead of the 'British' empirical tradition in both epistemology and politics, whose influence Russell traces forward through two centuries of European thought.

philosophers_discussed.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as the pivotal figure who revived the Continental, Cartesian-derived rationalist tradition after 1781, mistakenly believing he had synthesized it with Locke's empiricism; Russell also contrasts Kant's anti-utilitarian, 'noble' ethics with the Lockean/utilitarian line.

philosophers_discussed.name: George Berkeley
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as one of the two chief philosophical heirs of Locke, though (unlike Hume) 'politically unimportant' as a bishop uninterested in politics.

philosophers_discussed.name: David Hume
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as Locke's other chief philosophical heir; noted as a Tory whose reactionary political views (expressed in his History of England) show little direct connection between his empiricism and his politics, and whose personal residence in France helped transmit English influence there.

philosophers_discussed.name: Voltaire
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Identified as the principal transmitter of Locke's (and later Hume's) influence into eighteenth-century France, via his Lettres philosophiques.

philosophers_discussed.name: René Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as the fountainhead of the rival, Continental philosophical tradition (running through Spinoza and Leibniz to Kant and Hegel); his authority as a philosopher was diminished, Russell notes, when Newton's law of gravitation proved superior to his theory of vortices.

philosophers_discussed.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Used as Russell's example of the deductive, pyramid-building Continental method, illustrated by his monadology argument that, since matter is extended and therefore complex, and the simple cannot be extended, the ultimate constituents of things must be non-material, hence mental.

philosophers_discussed.name: Jeremy Bentham
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as a direct heir of Locke's tradition, part of the 'hard-headed' line of liberalism that Russell schematically traces (via Ricardo and Marx) toward Stalin.

philosophers_discussed.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Contrasted with Locke's moderate reformist followers as the inspiration for the 'extreme revolutionaries' among the French philosophes, and as founder of a rival, 'soft-hearted' line of thought that Russell schematically traces (via Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, Nietzsche) toward Hitler.

philosophers_discussed.name: Karl Marx
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as one of Locke's ultimate philosophical heirs (via Bentham and the Radicals), though Russell flags his system as too 'eclectic' for simple characterization and defers detailed treatment to a later chapter.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thomas Hobbes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the source of the 'power' strand of ethics opposed to the pleasure-based ethics of the empiricists, with Spinoza partly agreeing with him.

philosophers_discussed.name: Baruch Spinoza
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as holding two unreconciled ethical views, one (from Hobbes) valuing power, the other valuing mystic union with God; also named among the Continental rationalists whose metaphysical arguments for God Russell traces to the subject-predicate doctrine.

core_concepts.name: The two European philosophical traditions: British and Continental
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell divides post-Locke European philosophy into two families: a 'British' line (Locke, Berkeley, Hume, and later Mill) that reasons cautiously from many observed facts to modest conclusions, and a 'Continental' line (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, and later Kant and Hegel) that builds large, systematic conclusions from a few very general logical principles.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The British method draws 'a comparatively modest conclusion ... from a broad survey of many facts,' with a stable, base-heavy structure that can absorb local errors without total collapse; the Continental method 'pyramids' a vast edifice of deduction upon 'a pin-point of logical principle,' producing an unstable structure that total collapse if any part of the foundation is flawed.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This methodological contrast, for Russell, explains much of the substantive divergence between the two traditions on metaphysics (acceptance vs. rejection of a priori proofs of God), ethics (pleasure vs. 'noble' anti-utilitarian ends), and even politics (piecemeal reform vs. sweeping revolutionary or reactionary programmes).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced by Russell from Locke and Hume on one side, Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz on the other, surviving (he argues) even Kant's attempted synthesis.
examples: Hume's inductive handling of the 'missing shade of blue' objection to his own principle, which he treats as non-fatal because his method is empirical, not logical
Leibniz's monadology, deduced from the premise that whatever is complex must be composed of simples, which cannot be extended, hence not material, hence mental
competing_positions: Kant's own belief that he had synthesized the two traditions, which Russell rejects as historically false, since Kant's followers remained squarely in the Cartesian tradition
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Survives, per Russell, 'unvarying' from Descartes to Hegel on one side and from Locke to John Stuart Mill on the other, despite Kant's intervention.

core_concepts.name: The hard-headed and soft-hearted lines of post-Kantian liberalism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell sketches, half-seriously, two different paths that liberal ideas took after Rousseau and Kant: one 'hard-headed' line running through Bentham and Ricardo to Marx and eventually Stalin, and one 'soft-hearted' line running through Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, and Nietzsche to Hitler -- a deliberately schematic 'map and mnemonic' rather than a strict causal history.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's own words: 'Since Rousseau and Kant, there have been two schools of liberalism, which may be distinguished as the hard-headed and the soft-hearted. The hard-headed developed, through Bentham, Ricardo, and Marx, by logical stages into Stalin; the soft-hearted, by other logical stages, through Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, and Nietzsche, into Hitler.' Russell immediately qualifies this as 'too schematic to be quite true,' useful only 'as a map and a mnemonic.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Illustrates Russell's broader thesis that ideas do not develop by pure internal logic alone but are 'governed, throughout, by external circumstances and the reflection of these circumstances in human emotions' -- evidenced, he argues, by the fact that American liberalism, insulated from these European pressures, never underwent this development and remains 'to this day as in Locke.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: A retrospective interpretive scheme offered by Russell, writing during the Second World War, to characterize the political trajectories of Kantian/Rousseauian liberalism in Europe.
examples: American liberalism's continuity with Locke's original doctrines, unaffected by this European bifurcation
objections: Russell's own caveat that the scheme is 'too schematic to be quite true'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Deeply political; Russell explicitly frames this as history of ideas shaped by, not independent of, contemporary political emotion and circumstance.

core_concepts.name: Pleasure-based vs. 'noble' (anti-utilitarian) ethics
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke and the empiricist tradition held that pleasure or happiness is the good, and that ethics should aim at increasing it; their rationalist and idealist opponents (culminating in Kant) instead despised pleasure as an ignoble motive and prized things like duty, power, or heroic self-sacrifice as higher ends.
core_concepts.precise_definition: For Locke and his empiricist successors, pleasure was 'the good' throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; their opponents -- Hobbes (power), Spinoza (partly power, partly mystic union with God), Kant (duty performed for the moral law's own sake, with an afterlife needed to reconcile virtue and happiness) -- held ethics to a standard explicitly opposed to, or higher than, the pursuit of pleasure.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell argues, provocatively, that the men who thought happiness the end of life tended in practice to be the more benevolent and to do more to actually improve the world, while those who despised happiness as ignoble more often found, in 'noble' ideals like heroism, 'unconscious outlets for the impulse to power' and 'excuses for cruelty.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced through the whole post-Lockean tradition, culminating in Kant's explicitly anti-utilitarian ethics (Critique of Practical Reason).
examples: Kant's claim that helping your brother out of affection for him has no moral merit -- only acting because the moral law commands it does
Byron's heroes, prized for strong emotion (including hatred and revenge) rather than exemplary conduct
objections: Russell's own counter-argument: contempt for happiness is 'easier when the happiness is other people's than when it is our own'
competing_positions: Kant's ethics of duty, in which moral worth attaches only to acting from respect for the moral law, not from inclination or desire for pleasure
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell links the romantic, anti-utilitarian strand forward to Byron, Carlyle, and (in his schematic map) eventually to Nietzsche.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Kant's ethics requires postulating an afterlife and God to secure ultimate justice between virtue and happiness, since the virtuous often suffer in this world.

core_concepts.name: The obsolescence of Locke's individualist political philosophy
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Locke's political ideas worked well for a world of independent property-owning individuals, but Russell argues they became increasingly unable to handle the problems created by giant corporations, powerful nation-states, and total war between organized blocs rather than individuals.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Locke's political philosophy 'was, on the whole, adequate and useful until the industrial revolution'; since then, the growth of corporate economic power, expanding state functions (e.g., education), and the fusion of economic and political power through nationalism have left 'the single separate citizen' without 'the power and independence that he had in Locke's speculations,' so that 'our age is one of organization, and its conflicts are between organizations, not between separate individuals.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This closing argument extends Locke's own concept of the 'state of nature' (which, Locke says, persists between independent states) to argue that a genuine peace between nations requires something like 'a new international Social Contract,' after which much of Locke's political philosophy -- other than its treatment of private property -- could become applicable again.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's own concluding analysis, extending Locke's framework to twentieth-century conditions, written during the Second World War.
examples: The growth of vast corporations with power 'almost equal to those of the government,' especially in pre-Pearl-Harbor America
Nationalism's fusion of economic and political power, making war 'the principal means of competition'

arguments.title: Kant did not synthesize the British and Continental traditions
premises: Kant himself believed his critical philosophy synthesized the empirical tradition (from Locke) and the rationalist tradition (from Descartes).
Historically, however, the philosophers who developed and followed Kant (German idealism, Hegel and his successors) remained squarely within the Cartesian, not the Lockean, tradition.

The characteristic methodological difference between the two traditions -- piecemeal induction vs. deductive system-building -- persisted unchanged 'from Descartes to Hegel on the one side, and from Locke to John Stuart Mill on the other.'
arguments.conclusion: Kant's self-understanding as a synthesizer of empiricism and rationalism cannot be sustained from a historical point of view; his actual legacy belongs to the Continental line.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses this claim to organize the whole chapter's account of post-Lockean philosophy into two persisting, largely separate streams, despite Kant's intervening attempt at unification.
implications: Frames the subsequent contrast Russell draws between British/empiricist and Continental/idealist metaphysics, ethics, and politics

arguments.title: The link between happiness-based ethics and practical benevolence
premises: Ethical systems that prize something other than happiness (e.g., heroism, power, strong emotion, duty for its own sake) are, in practice, easier to hold with indifference or even cruelty toward others' suffering.
A person's ethical theory tends to reflect and reinforce their underlying character.
Historically, those who explicitly valued happiness as the good tended to act more benevolently and did more to improve human welfare than those who scorned happiness as ignoble.
arguments.conclusion: The utilitarian, Lockean tradition of valuing happiness, despite its philosophical unfashionableness among 'noble' anti-utilitarians, did more good in practice than its rivals.
arguments.explanation: Russell offers this as a pointed, evaluative aside rather than a strictly demonstrated thesis, using it to connect the abstract ethical divide between the two traditions to concrete historical and political consequences (including, implicitly, the rise of fascism from the 'soft-hearted,' anti-utilitarian line).
implications: Colors Russell's broader normative preference, visible throughout the book, for the empiricist/utilitarian tradition over its rationalist/idealist rivals

key_distinctions: British (inductive, piecemeal) method vs. Continental (deductive, systematic) method
Pleasure/happiness as the good vs. 'noble,' anti-utilitarian ends (power, duty, heroism)
Hard-headed liberalism (Bentham, Ricardo, Marx) vs. soft-hearted liberalism (Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, Nietzsche) -- Russell's own schematic distinction
Locke's political philosophy as adequate to an age of individuals vs. its obsolescence in an age of organizations and nation-states
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The chapter is essentially retrospective, tracing Locke's own debts (already discussed in the two preceding chapters) forward, while explicitly contrasting the Lockean line with the Cartesian line running back through Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell traces Locke's heirs as, first, Berkeley and Hume; second, the French philosophes outside Rousseau's circle; third, Bentham and the philosophical Radicals; and fourth (with Continental additions) Marx and his followers -- while the rival Cartesian-Kantian line runs to Hegel and, in Russell's schematic political mapping, toward twentieth-century totalitarianism on both the left (via Bentham, Ricardo, Marx to Stalin) and right (via Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, Nietzsche to Hitler).
political_social_context: Russell stresses that until the French Revolution, English followers of Locke (Berkeley, Hume) took little interest in politics, since England was politically quiescent; the Revolution forced philosophers generally into political engagement. He also notes the peculiar case of American liberalism, which, insulated from the European pressures (the guillotine, Napoleon, German nationalism) that drove the 'hard-headed'/'soft-hearted' bifurcation, remained essentially unchanged from Locke's own doctrines.
religion_science_culture_context: Russell notes the initial European victory of Locke's philosophy over Descartes' owed as much to Newton's triumph over Descartes' physics (the law of gravitation defeating the theory of vortices) as to purely philosophical argument, while after 1792 the empirical tradition was blamed, especially in reaction, for the excesses of the French Revolution, driving 'recanting revolutionaries such as Coleridge' toward Kant.
russell_presentation: Russell uses this short chapter as a hinge, closing the discussion of Locke by mapping the whole subsequent development of European philosophy onto the opposition between Locke's empirical, piecemeal 'British' method and the deductive, systematic 'Continental' method descending from Descartes. He credits historical accident as much as logical necessity for Locke's initial European triumph (Newton's defeat of Descartes' physics; French intellectuals' admiration for English liberty), and treats Kant's claimed synthesis of the two traditions as a historical illusion, since Kant's own followers remained Cartesian in spirit. Russell then extends the contrast into ethics, favoring the pleasure/happiness-based line associated with Locke over 'noble,' anti-utilitarian rivals, and offers his provocative, explicitly schematic 'hard-headed'/'soft-hearted' map linking Kantian and Rousseauian liberalism, through very different logical developments, to Stalin and Hitler respectively -- a claim he immediately flags as too simple to be strictly true. The chapter ends by arguing that Locke's individualist political philosophy, though 'adequate and useful until the industrial revolution,' has been outstripped by an age of corporations, nation-states, and organized conflict, and can only be fully restored by an eventual international social contract.
critical_context: Russell's own methodological caveat, stated explicitly in the text, functions as its own critical context: his 'hard-headed'/'soft-hearted' historical map from Kant/Rousseau to Stalin/Hitler is offered as 'too schematic to be quite true,' useful only as 'a map and a mnemonic' rather than a rigorous causal history -- a self-aware simplification later historians of ideas have often flagged as one of the more speculative and contestable passages in this part of the book.
key_takeaways: Russell divides post-Locke European philosophy into two enduring traditions: the empirical, piecemeal 'British' line (Locke, Berkeley, Hume, Mill) and the deductive, systematic 'Continental' line (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Kant, Hegel).
Locke's early triumph in England and France owed as much to Newton's defeat of Cartesian physics and to French admiration for English liberty as to purely philosophical argument.
Kant believed he had synthesized the two traditions, but Russell argues his actual followers remained within the Cartesian, not the Lockean, line.

The pleasure-based ethics of Locke's tradition is contrasted with 'noble,' anti-utilitarian ethics (Hobbes's power, Kant's duty); Russell argues the former did more, in practice, to increase human happiness.

Russell's schematic 'hard-headed' (Bentham-Ricardo-Marx-Stalin) and 'soft-hearted' (Fichte-Byron-Carlyle-Nietzsche-Hitler) lines of post-Kantian liberalism are explicitly flagged as an oversimplified mnemonic, not strict causal history.
American liberalism, insulated from the European pressures driving this bifurcation, remained closer to Locke's original doctrines.

Locke's individualist political philosophy is presented as increasingly inadequate to an age of corporations and nation-states, resolvable, in Russell's view, only by an eventual international social contract.
study_notes:
This chapter functions as a bridge: it looks backward, tying together the epistemological Locke of Chapter XIII and the political Locke of Chapter XIV, and it looks forward, previewing the two philosophical streams -- British empiricism and Continental rationalism -- that will structure much of the rest of Russell's account of modern philosophy (Berkeley and Hume on one side; Kant, Hegel, and their successors on the other).

The most important analytical tool in the chapter is Russell's contrast of methods, not just doctrines: the British 'pyramid' rests on a broad base of observed fact and tapers upward, so a single flawed observation rarely brings the whole structure down, while the Continental 'pyramid' balances a vast structure on a single sharp logical point, so one flawed premise can collapse everything. Keep this image in mind when you reach the later chapters on Leibniz, Kant, and Hegel.

Be careful, however, to register Russell's own repeated caveats about how schematic some of his claims are -- especially the 'hard-headed'/'soft-hearted' genealogy connecting Kant and Rousseau, through many intermediate figures, to Stalin and Hitler. Russell explicitly calls this 'too schematic to be quite true' and offers it only as 'a map and a mnemonic,' which is a useful reminder that even a historian as confident as Russell sometimes flags his own broad-brush generalizations as provisional rather than rigorously demonstrated.

Finally, notice how the chapter's closing argument -- that Locke's individualism has been outstripped by an age of corporations and nation-states -- reflects Russell's own historical moment, writing in the middle of the Second World War, and gives the seemingly dry seventeenth-century material immediate, current stakes.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The line of philosophers, from Locke through Hume to Mill, who build modest conclusions carefully from lots of observed facts.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's label for the inductive, piecemeal philosophical method running from Locke through Berkeley, Hume, and J. S. Mill, characterized by drawing cautious conclusions from broad empirical surveys.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The line of philosophers, from Descartes through Leibniz to Kant and Hegel, who build huge logical systems from just a few starting principles.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's label for the deductive, systematic philosophical method running from Descartes through Spinoza and Leibniz to Kant and Hegel, characterized by 'pyramiding' extensive conclusions on a small number of a priori principles.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Russell's label (half-joking) for one branch of post-Kantian liberal thought that, he schematically suggests, led eventually toward Stalin.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's schematic characterization of the liberal line running through Bentham, Ricardo, and Marx.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Russell's label (half-joking) for the other branch of post-Kantian liberal thought that, he schematically suggests, led eventually toward Hitler.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's schematic characterization of the liberal line running through Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, and Nietzsche.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: An approach to ethics that looks down on ordinary pleasure and happiness as unworthy goals, favoring things like heroism or duty instead.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's term for ethical systems (e.g., Kant's) that reject pleasure/happiness as the good in favor of ostensibly higher ends such as duty or heroic self-sacrifice.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, who are Locke's first two, most direct philosophical heirs?
questions.explanation: Russell names Berkeley and Hume as the first two links in the chain of Locke's philosophical heirs, followed by the non-Rousseauian philosophes, Bentham and the Radicals, and eventually Marx.

questions.prompt: What historical/scientific event does Russell credit, alongside purely philosophical argument, for Locke's early victory over Descartes in England and France?
questions.answer: Newton's law of gravitation proving superior to Descartes' theory of vortices as an explanation of the solar system, which diminished respect for Descartes and increased respect for England.
questions.explanation: Russell stresses that intellectual victories are often driven by such 'illogical' historical factors as much as by argument.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher believed he had synthesized the empirical philosophy of Locke and the rationalist philosophy of Descartes, a claim Russell rejects historically?
questions.explanation: Russell argues that, historically, Kant's own followers remained in the Cartesian rather than the Lockean tradition.

questions.prompt: Contrast the 'British' and 'Continental' philosophical methods as Russell describes them, using Hume and Leibniz as examples.
questions.answer: Hume's British method draws a modest conclusion from a broad survey of facts and treats apparent counter-examples (like the missing shade of blue) as non-fatal, since his principle is empirical. Leibniz's Continental method deduces a vast conclusion (that all things are ultimately non-material 'monads,' i.e., souls) from a single logical principle about simples and complexity, so that any flaw in that one principle would collapse the whole system.
questions.explanation: This contrast is the chapter's central analytical tool for understanding the divergence of post-Lockean philosophy.

questions.prompt: What does Russell mean by calling his account of 'hard-headed' and 'soft-hearted' liberalism 'too schematic to be quite true'?
questions.answer: He means the neat genealogies he draws -- Bentham/Ricardo/Marx leading logically to Stalin, and Fichte/Byron/Carlyle/Nietzsche leading logically to Hitler -- are a simplified mnemonic device for orientation, not a rigorously demonstrated causal history.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly flags this passage as a deliberate simplification, 'a map and a mnemonic.'

questions.prompt: How does Kant's ethics differ from the pleasure-based ethics of the Lockean tradition, according to this chapter?
questions.answer: Kant holds that an act has moral merit only when performed because the moral law commands it, not from inclination (e.g., fondness for a family member); he also holds that, since the virtuous often suffer in this life, there must be another world and a God to secure ultimate justice -- a sharply anti-utilitarian, 'noble' ethic opposed to the Lockean view that pleasure/happiness is the good.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this contrast to argue, provocatively, that the happiness-valuing tradition did more good in practice than its 'noble' rivals.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's argument for why Locke's political philosophy has become inadequate since the industrial revolution.
questions.answer: Locke's political philosophy assumed independent, roughly equal individual citizens as the basic political unit; but since the industrial revolution, economic power has concentrated in vast corporations, state functions (like education) have expanded enormously, and nationalism has fused economic and political power, making organized conflict between states and blocs (not individuals) the norm -- conditions Locke's framework did not anticipate and cannot fully address without an eventual international social contract.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's closing argument, extending Locke's own 'state of nature' concept to relations between modern states.

quiz.related_concept: The obsolescence of Locke's individualist political philosophy

quiz.prompt: Match each ethical stance to its representative: (1) pleasure/happiness as the good, (2) power as the good, (3) duty for the moral law's own sake.
quiz.explanation: Locke and the empiricist tradition held pleasure/happiness to be the good; Hobbes valued power; Kant held that only acting from duty (the moral law) has moral merit.

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Russell's 'British' and 'Continental' philosophical methods, using Hume and Leibniz as representative examples. Which method do you find more epistemically sound, and why?
rubric: Correct use of the Hume and Leibniz examples

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's claim that thinkers who valued happiness/pleasure as the ethical good tended, in practice, to do more to increase human welfare than those who valued 'nobler' ends like heroism or duty. Is this a fair generalization?
rubric: Consideration of counter-examples on both sides
Discussion of Kant's ethics as the chapter's key contrast case

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Russell's argument that Locke's individualist political philosophy became inadequate after the industrial revolution. Does his proposed remedy -- an international social contract -- follow naturally from Locke's own premises?
rubric: Accurate summary of Russell's argument about obsolescence
Clear explanation of the 'state of nature between states' extension
Assessment of whether an international social contract is a natural extension of Locke's framework
